title: Completion of finite-type schemes and adic base change
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative Noetherian ring, $K\subset A$ an ideal, and suppose $A\cong\varprojlim_n A/K^n$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. For a finite-type $A$-scheme $Z$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], its completion along $K\mathcal O_Z$, as a ringed space, is obtained by completing its affine charts; an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}C$ becomes $\operatorname{Spf}\widehat C_{KC}$. Here $\operatorname{Spf}R$ has the primes containing its ideal of definition and the inverse-limit structure sheaf [def-per-adic-formal-geometry]. This completion is a Noetherian adic formal scheme. Morphisms of finite-type $A$-schemes induce completion morphisms functorially, and open immersions induce formal open immersions. If $A\to B$ is a homomorphism to a Noetherian ring complete for $KB$, then there is a canonical isomorphism
$$\widehat{(Z\times_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\operatorname{Spec}B)}_{K}\ \cong\ \widehat Z_K\times_{\operatorname{Spf}A}\operatorname{Spf}B.$$
The fibre product here is the fibre product of adic formal schemes: on an affine chart it is the formal spectrum of the completed tensor product
$$\widehat C_{KC}\widehat\otimes_A B:=\varprojlim_{n\ge1}\bigl((\widehat C_{KC}/K^n\widehat C_{KC})\otimes_{A/K^n}(B/K^nB)\bigr)\ \cong\ \widehat{(C\otimes_A B)}_K.$$
The tensor product is the commutative algebra tensor product, with multiplication $(c\otimes b)(c'\otimes b')=cc'\otimes bb'$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The displayed isomorphisms are induced by the coefficient maps, are natural in $Z$ and $B$, commute with principal-open restrictions on either side, and respect the ideals extended from $Z$. For a second complete Noetherian adic algebra $B\to D$, the two successive comparisons agree with the direct comparison for $A\to D$. On formal affine charts, morphisms $\operatorname{Spf}S\to\operatorname{Spf}R$ correspond precisely to continuous ring homomorphisms $R\to S$.

proof.text: Choose a finite affine cover of $Z$ by $U_i=\operatorname{Spec}C_i$, with each $C_i$ a finite-type $A$-algebra, using the definition of finite type. Each $C_i$ is Noetherian by the finite-type algebra theorem. Write $I_i=KC_i$ and $R_i=\varprojlim_n C_i/I_i^n$. Completion is Noetherian and complete, and its projection onto $C_i/I_i^n$ is surjective with kernel $I_i^nR_i$, by the cited completion results. Thus $R_i/I_i^nR_i=C_i/I_i^n$, canonically and compatibly with reduction. The same argument works on any affine chart: $Z$ is Noetherian by finite-type permanence, and its affine coordinate ring is Noetherian by the affine-open lemma. All ideals used here are finitely generated because these rings are Noetherian.

On $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$, put $I=KC$ and $R=\widehat C_I$. The completion definition has space $V(I)$ and sheaf the inverse limit of the quotient-scheme sheaves. The canonical isomorphisms $C/I^n=R/I^nR$ of Step 1 identify this ringed space with $\operatorname{Spf}R$: they identify the prime spaces, and the sheaves agree sectionwise. The index category of positive integers is small; the sectionwise-limit lemma applies to the underlying sheaves of sets, with ring operations defined componentwise. On $D(c)$ the sections are $\varprojlim_n(C/I^n)_c=\widehat{C_c}_{IC_c}$, using localization modulo an ideal. The formal principal-chart lemma identifies this with the corresponding formal open of $\operatorname{Spf}R$. Hence these identifications agree on all open overlaps, by their agreement on a principal basis. The completion is therefore covered by the finitely many $\operatorname{Spf}R_i$ and is a Noetherian adic formal scheme. No intersection of two affine opens is assumed affine.

proof.text: Here and below formal morphisms are continuous local morphisms of topologically ringed spaces. We prove the affine morphism assertion. Let $R,S$ be complete Noetherian rings with ideals of definition $I,J$, and let $\phi:R\to S$ be continuous. For each $m$ choose $n(m)$ with $\phi(I^{n(m)})\subseteq J^m$. The induced affine-scheme maps $\operatorname{Spec}(S/J^m)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R/I^{n(m)})$ give one continuous map of prime spaces: inverse image of $\mathfrak q$ is $\phi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. On a principal open $D(r)$ they give maps $(R/I^{n(m)})_r\to(S/J^m)_{\phi(r)}$. Passing to compatible sequences defines the continuous map of completed section rings. Independence of $n(m)$ follows by increasing it and reducing; agreement on smaller principal opens follows by localizing the same quotient map. These maps define a sheaf morphism. It is local on stalks: a germ of a section is a unit exactly when its reduction on the closed fibre is a unit at the point. Indeed, after shrinking to a principal neighbourhood an inverse modulo the defining ideal lifts to an inverse by the convergent geometric series $1+e+e^2+\cdots$ for an error $e$ in that ideal. Conversely a unit stays a unit on the closed fibre. The quotient-scheme maps are local, so the resulting morphism is local.

proof.text: Conversely a formal morphism $f:\operatorname{Spf}S\to\operatorname{Spf}R$ gives a continuous homomorphism $\phi:R\to S$ on global sections, since the principal-section formula at $1$ identifies these section rings with $R,S$. Locality and the unit criterion proved in Step 3 force $f(\mathfrak q)=\phi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$, and thus $f^{-1}D(r)=D(\phi(r))$. Its map on these sections extends $R_r\to S_{\{\phi(r)\}}$ with $a/r^k\mapsto\phi(a)/\phi(r)^k$. This extension is unique: $R_r$ surjects onto every $(R/I^n)_r$, hence is dense in $R_{\{r\}}$, while $S_{\{\phi(r)\}}$ is separated. More explicitly, for any target power $J^m$, continuity lets us compute the image of a section using a representative modulo a sufficiently large $I^n$; two representatives have the same image modulo $J^m$. All $m$ determine the image. These are exactly the maps of Step 3, so the constructions are inverse. Applying the completion construction to the maps on $Z_n=Z\times_A A/K^n$ gives functoriality for scheme morphisms. It respects identities and composition at every quotient. Restricting to an open simply restricts the same space and sheaf, so an open immersion completes to a formal open immersion.

proof.text:
Fix $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ as in Step 1 and write $R=\widehat C_{KC}$, $E=C\otimes_A B$. The algebra $E$ is finite type over $B$: if $c_1,\ldots,c_r$ generate $C$ over $A$, then $c_i\otimes1$ generate $E$ over $B$. Therefore $E$ is Noetherian, and $P=\widehat E_{KE}$ is Noetherian and complete. For each $n$ the quotient theorem of Step 1 gives $R/K^nR=C/K^nC$. There is a canonical ring isomorphism
$$(R/K^nR)\otimes_{A/K^n}(B/K^nB)\simeq E/K^nE.$$
Its forward map sends $\bar c\otimes\bar b$ to $[c\otimes b]$. Its inverse sends $[c\otimes b]$ to $\bar c\otimes\bar b$. The tensor pushout property supplies these ring maps: they are well defined because the images of $K^n$ vanish and the two coefficient maps agree on $A$. The composites are identities on both coefficient rings, hence on their tensor product. Reduction in $n$ commutes with both formulas. Taking compatible sequences gives exactly the displayed completed-tensor-product isomorphism $R\widehat\otimes_A B\simeq P$. Ordinary affine fibre products identify $U\times_A B$ with $\operatorname{Spec}E$, so Step 2 identifies its completion with $\operatorname{Spf}P$.

We check the formal fibre-product universal property, rather than interchange tensor product and inverse limit. For a formal affine test object $\operatorname{Spf}(T,J)$, Steps 3–4 turn a pair of maps to $\operatorname{Spf}R$ and $\operatorname{Spf}B$ over $\operatorname{Spf}A$ into continuous maps $\alpha:R\to T$ and $\beta:B\to T$ agreeing on $A$. The tensor universal property gives $h:E\to T$, $h(c\otimes b)=\alpha(c)\beta(b)$. For each $m$, continuity of $\beta$ gives an $n$ with $h(K^nE)\subseteq J^m$. Thus $E/K^nE\to T/J^m$ defines a map $P\to T/J^m$ by projection from $P$; increasing $n$ leaves it unchanged. These maps are compatible in $m$ and hence give $P\to\varprojlim_mT/J^m=T$. This map is continuous, since it annihilates $K^nP$ modulo $J^m$, and extends $h$. It is unique by the same quotient-representative argument as in Step 4, since $E$ is dense in $P$. Its restriction to $R$ is $\alpha$ since both maps agree on dense $C$; its restriction to $B$ is $\beta$. Conversely any continuous map $P\to T$ gives this pair. Steps 3–4 now identify $\operatorname{Spf}P$ as the formal fibre product on affine test objects. For arbitrary formal test objects cover by formal affines and glue these uniquely determined maps; uniqueness on overlaps follows after an affine refinement.

proof.text: On a principal open of a $C$-chart, the comparison of Step 5 has the same formulas with $c$ inverted; on a principal open of the $B$-side it has the same formulas with $b$ inverted. Localization commutes with quotient, and the tensor pushout property identifies the localized tensors, since the indicated coefficient is made invertible on both sides. Consequently all the finite-level comparison maps commute with these restrictions. Passing to compatible sequences and using the formal principal-chart lemma proves compatibility with formal principal opens. Cover an arbitrary overlap by principal opens inside each chart; the comparisons there are the maps induced by the same two coefficient maps, so they agree by the uniqueness in Step 6. The formal gluing lemma now gives the global comparison isomorphism. Its inverse glues from the inverse formulas of Step 5. The fibre-product universal property is local on the source by that same gluing lemma, so the global comparison is the asserted formal fibre product.

All maps above are specified on the coefficient elements $c\otimes1$ and $1\otimes b$ and on every quotient by $K^n$. A morphism of $Z$ or a further coefficient map carries these elements to their named images; both orders around each naturality square do exactly that. The tensor uniqueness proves equality at each finite quotient, and equality of every projection proves equality of the maps on completions. For $A\to B\to D$, both the iterated and direct comparisons therefore send $c$ to $c\otimes1$ and $d$ to $1\otimes d$ in $\widehat{C\otimes_A D}$; equivalently both are the unique map of the same fibre-product cone. This proves the composition clause. If $H\subseteq C$ is an ideal from $Z$, both sides carry its extended ideal to the ideal generated by exactly the same elements $h\otimes1$ ($h\in H$); inverses give equality, and the restriction compatibility in Step 7 glues it. Thus ideals are respected as well. These arguments include $K=0$, nilpotent $K$, empty charts, and the zero ring.
